articles.title: Meta Tags for SEO: What They Are, Why They Matter, and How to Use Them
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Meta tags are HTML snippets in the <head> section of your page that tell search engines and AI tools what your content is about. 
  • Human readers don’t see meta tags directly, but the tags shape how your pages show up in search and social previews. 
  • Not all meta tags for SEO move the needle. The title tag, canonical, and robots meta tag directly affect SEO. Meta descriptions, viewport, and Open Graph tags contribute indirectly through click-through rate (CTR), mobile usability, and social sharing. 
  • Google rewrites roughly 76 percent of title tags it analyzes, so a well-optimized title still matters even when Google might overwrite it. 
  • The same meta tag hygiene that helps you rank in Google can also improve visibility in AI-powered features like Google AI Overviews, since AI parsers rely on structured signals to interpret and cite your pages. 
  • Meta tags decay over time. Run a full audit at least quarterly, or after any major site migration or content management system (CMS) update.

What does the term “meta tags” cover, and which ones matter for SEO?

Some of the advice out there is outdated, and plenty of tags that sound important don’t really affect your rankings.

This guide covers the meta tags for SEO that influence how search engines and AI tools read your pages. I’ll walk you through what each tag does and how to implement them correctly. I’ll also show you which tags you can safely ignore and how to audit your meta tag setup to strengthen your visibility across traditional and AI search.

What Are Meta Tags?

Meta tags are a type of HTML tag that provides search engines with information about a website page.

Two tags do most of the work: your title tag and meta description.

Your title and meta description tags create the cover for your web page. They’re the first impression most visitors get about your site. That’s where the importance of meta tags in SEO lies. They’re the elements that control how your pages appear in search.

Meta tags shape so much of your site’s visibility, yet they operate entirely behind the scenes. They live in the <head> HTML section of your site’s source code. They’re invisible to visitors but instrumental in explaining the content and structure of your pages to search engines, browsers, and social media platforms.

By Mark Mwachiro This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of Aug. 24, 2026.

MS NOW reported week-to-week gains in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo during prime time and total day. The network should be especially pleased with its primetime performance, as it was up by double digits in both measured categories.

Meanwhile, Fox News, which led all networks, was down in the primetime demo and in total viewers and the demo during total day. As for CNN, it shed total viewers during total day.

According to Nielsen big data + panel for the week of Aug. 24, Fox News averaged 2.027 million total viewers and 169,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network was up by +1% in total viewers but had a -5% slide in the demo compared to the week prior ( the week beginning August 17 ).

During total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.257 million total viewers and 104,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on its average from the previous week’s measurements, the network declined by -2% in total viewers and -8% in the demo.

Fox News continued to rank first in total primetime viewership and dropped from third to fourth place in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it also finished first in total viewers and was No. 2 in the total day demo.

MS NOW averaged 937,000 total viewers and 80,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. The network grew by +10% in total viewers and +21% in the demo compared to its primetime average the prior week.

During total day, MS NOW averaged 596,000 total viewers and 56,000 demo viewers. It was up +4% in total viewers and +17% in the demo compared to the network’s average the week prior.

Among all basic cable networks, MS NOW moved from third to second place in total primetime viewers and was 15th in the demo. It also ranked third in total viewers and climbed one spot to 11th in the total day demo.

CNN averaged 611,000 total primetime viewers and 113,000 demo viewers. It gained +5% in total viewers and +8% in the demo compared to the previous week.

During total day, the network had 400,000 total viewers and 61,000 viewers in the demo. CNN was down by -1% in total viewers but grew by +2% in the demo during this daypart.

Among all cable networks, CNN finished sixth in total viewers and dropped to 11th from 10th in the demo during primetime. It remained at No. 4 in total day among total viewers and was No. 9 in the demo.

When looking at these networks’ performance during the same period a year ago :

During primetime, Fox News was down -3% in total viewers and -22% in the A25-54 demo. During total day, the network was down -9% in total viewers and -31% in the demo—the only network with year to year losses within this comparison.

MS NOW was up +27% in total viewers and +19% in the demo. During total day, the network was up +21% in total viewers and +19% in the demo.

articles.title: 12 best social media monitoring tools for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media monitoring tools track brand mentions, competitor activity, and audience sentiment across social platforms and the wider web in real time.
  2. The best social media monitoring tools combine broad platform coverage, fast alerts, accurate sentiment analysis, and integrations with your existing tech stack.
  3. Monitoring and listening serve different purposes: monitoring catches what’s being said right now, while listening analyzes trends over time to inform strategy.
  4. To get the most value, make monitoring a daily habit, customize your keyword tracking, and pair tool insights with human judgment.

What is social media monitoring?

Social media monitoring is the process of tracking mentions of your brand, products, competitors, or industry across social platforms. It involves following specific hashtags, keywords, and direct mentions to understand how your brand is being perceived.

Bonus: Download a free guide to learn how to use social media monitoring to boost sales and conversions today. No tricks or boring tips—just simple, easy-to-follow instructions that really work.

Social media monitoring vs. social listening

Social media monitoring vs social listening comes down to depth. Monitoring focuses on tracking data, while social listening goes a step further by analyzing what the data means.

Let’s take a closer look at their differences:

The most effective strategies use both. Monitoring helps you stay responsive in the moment, while listening helps you understand the bigger picture and plan next steps.

What are social media monitoring tools?

Social media monitoring tools help marketers track conversations, mentions, and trends across platforms, now reaching 5.75 billion users globally, in real time.

Katelyn Rhoades, Founder of the social media marketing agency Enfluence Marketing Studio, says that social media monitoring tools are crucial for making data-driven decisions.

By Robert Klara The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

As further confirmation of Americans’ interest in better-for-you food options—and legacy brands’ eagerness to snap up agile upstarts—Barilla has announced its intent to purchase mac and cheese brand Goodles. Financial terms were not disclosed.

In a statement, Barilla Group chairman Guido Barilla said that he’d “been following Goodles closely for some time” and has been “impressed by the strength of the brand, the quality of its products, and the momentum behind its growth.”

Goodles’ parent Gooder Foods is a six-year-old company founded by entrepreneurs Jen Zeszut and Paul Earle. (Wonder Woman star Gal Gadot and husband Jaron Varsano are also co-founders.) Starting off as a direct-to-consumer brand before securing shelf space at Target, Walmart and Costco, Goodles has taken aim at a category that, while indisputably big (mac and cheese is a $5.5 billion market in America), is not known for innovation.

While perhaps not “healthy” as such, Goodles positions itself as a more attractive alternative to established box brands by being higher in protein and fiber, and offering more interesting flavors thanks to ingredients like black tuffles, pesto, and hatch chiles.

Goodles is pricey compared to Kraft Mac & Cheese ( $3.79 vs. $1.39 at Target) and represents a premium in a category where store brands have been stealing market share and rock-bottom prices are the norm. According to research from Innova Market Insights, historically, American consumers are not willing to pay premium prices for pasta.

However, the mac and cheese segment is growing by 4.5% yearly, according to data from Insight Partners, and Goodles claims it’s “proving that mac and cheese is not just for kids anymore and is driving significant incrementality for all of its retail partners.”

One wild card remains GLP-1s, whose ability to curb appetites is bad news for convenience foods, but possibly good news for Goodles, which boasts 21 plant-based nutrients.

Founded in 1877, privately held Barilla is the largest pasta producer in the world, with 2025 revenues of $5.6 billion.

Robert Klara is the senior editor of brands at Adweek, specializing in the evolution and impact of brands.

articles.title: How to find your social media target audience in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. A social media target audience is the specific group of people most likely to engage with your brand on social, defined by demographics, interests, behaviors, and stage in the customer journey.
  2. Your social media audience is not the same as your target market. Most brands need several audience segments across different platforms and campaigns.
  3. Analytics, social listening, and competitor analysis are the most reliable ways to identify and refine who you are actually reaching.
  4. Reaching your audience means matching platform, format, and message to each segment, then testing and adjusting based on performance data.

What is a social media target audience?

A social media target audience is a specific group of people your brand wants to reach on social media, based on shared traits like interests, behaviors, and demographics.

These are the users most likely to engage with your content, respond to your messaging, and convert into customers.

It is worth separating this from your general marketing audience. Someone might be a perfect customer for your product and still never see a single post, because they do not use the platforms you publish on or engage with the formats you produce. Your social media audience is defined as much by platform behavior as by buying potential.

For example, Momofuku Goods shares recipes modified for home cooks on their Instagram account. Of course, they incorporate Momofuku Goods products, but the recipes address a core interest of its audience.

Source: Momofukugoods

Understanding their target audience’s interest in cooking is a major contributing factor explaining why the Goods brand itself has over 182,000 followers.

In short: Your social media target audience is the slice of people you can realistically reach, and reliably engage, on the platforms where you publish.

Download now!

Social media target audience vs. target market: What is the difference?

A target market is the broad group of potential customers for your product or service, while a social media target audience is the narrower subset you aim to reach with a specific campaign or on a specific platform.

The target market is a business decision. The target audience is a channel decision. A running shoe brand might define its target market as recreational runners aged 25 to 55 in North America. On TikTok, its target audience might be first-time marathon trainees aged 22 to 30 who follow race-day content. Same company, much tighter group.

The simplest way to hold the difference: Your target market tells you who to sell to, and your social media target audience tells you who to talk to today.

Why does defining your social media target audience matter?

Defining your audience matters because it determines where your budget goes, what you publish, and whether any of it produces results you can measure.

Broad targeting feels safe, but it usually means diluted messaging, wasted paid spend, and content that no single group finds particularly relevant. A clearly defined audience gives you:

  • Focused messaging: You write for a specific person instead of a hypothetical average, which makes content sharper and easier to produce at scale.
  • Better return on spend: Narrow ad targeting reduces wasted impressions and improves the efficiency of every campaign dollar. It also makes your social media ROI easier to attribute.
  • Smarter platform selection: Knowing where your audience already spends time keeps teams from maintaining channels that never deliver.
  • Stronger brand relationships: Relevance compounds. People who consistently see content that matches their interests are far more likely to stick around.

For larger teams, there is a governance benefit too. When audience definitions are documented and shared as part of your broader social strategy, regional teams and agencies stay consistent instead of interpreting the brand differently on every channel.

What are the types of social media target audiences?

Social media target audiences are usually grouped by one of five approaches: demographics, psychographics, behavioral signals, purchase intent, or existing customer status. Most brands use a combination rather than picking just one.

Here are the main types of audience segmentation to work with:

  • Demographics
  • Psychographics
  • Behavioral signals
  • Purchase intent
  • Existing customers

Demographics

Demographics cover age, gender, level of education, location, and income level. They are the easiest data to pull and the easiest place to start, since every native analytics tool reports them.

One caveat worth repeating: Your social media target audience may not share the same demographics as your target audience for other marketing efforts. The people who buy from you and the people who follow you are often two overlapping but distinct groups.

Using AI involves a surprising amount of copying and pasting. You pull numbers from a dashboard, drop them into a chat, and then ask your question. 

An MCP (or Model Context Protocol) cuts out those extra steps, helping social marketers work with AI in a way that feels less clunky. Let’s look at how it works, what it can do, and what social teams should know before plugging in.

What is a social media MCP?

A social media MCP creates a connection between an AI assistant (like Claude or ChatGPT) and the tools your social media team already uses.

Normally, an AI assistant only knows what you paste into the chat. Want to analyze your top-performing posts from last month? You have to dig up the data yourself, copy it over, and hope you didn’t miss anything.

An MCP skips those steps. It lets the assistant follow you across all of your tools, including your content calendar, analytics, and social listening data.

Do it better with Hootsuite, the all-in-one social media tool. Stay on top of things, grow, and beat the competition.

How does MCP differ from a social media API?

An API is basically the invisible plumbing that lets two tools talk to each other. The catch is that a developer usually has to connect each AI tool with custom code.

An MCP, on the other hand, hands the AI assistant a menu of available tools, plus instructions for how to use them. The assistant then chooses the right tool for each task.

“The practical difference is that you’re not writing custom integration code for every new tool,” says Lily Tewolde, AI Product Manager at Mela AI, “and the model can chain several together to finish one task.”

Why does MCP matter for social media teams?

With MCP, AI assistants can plug into the tools your social team already uses, giving them real context instead of information you feed them manually.

Here’s where that pays off:

It cuts down busywork

Getting social data into an AI chatbot can sometimes feel like a mini admin project. Export the report. Upload the file. Ask your question. Then do it all again next week.

With MCP, your assistant already has access to what’s sitting inside your social tools. No more explaining your entire social strategy — or uploading yet another spreadsheet — every time you open a new chat. 

It makes AI responses more useful

Without access to your actual social media data, an AI chatbot can only offer generic advice. Useful, maybe. Specific to your brand? Not so much.

MCP gives your assistant real context to work with. For example, it can pull your top-performing posts from your analytics, or spot gaps in your content calendar.

That means more answers grounded in your actual content, audience, and performance.

It can bring more of your workflow into a single chat

Social work has never lived in one place. You might check analytics in one dashboard, manage your content calendar in another, and open a blank document when it’s time to write.

MCP lets the assistant collaborate across all of your tools. Check last week’s numbers, get a few campaign ideas, and draft the posts, all from the same chat.

A social media MCP helps your AI assistant work with your actual social data and tools, so it can brainstorm better content ideas, schedule posts across platforms, answer analytics questions, build reports, and more.

Most of the time, brainstorming with an AI assistant starts with a blank chat. MCP gives it something better to work with: your actual social data.

articles.title: AI Slop Cleanup Job Listings Up 87%, Report Says via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
Job listings for correcting AI-generated work increased by 87% on Freelancer.com from August 2025 to June 2026, totaling 10,760 posts globally, according to internal platform data the Guardian reported today.

Upwork data shared with the outlet showed a 70% year-over-year rise in AI remediation gigs, meaning jobs fixing AI output. Fiverr noted that searches for “AI cleanup” services grew more than 20-fold from 2023 to 2026. The report highlights designers, writers, and video editors who now spend much of their time refining outputs from tools like ChatGPT and Claude. Their common complaint is that clients often budget these repairs as quick and inexpensive, even though the work may require as much effort as starting anew.

Freelancer.com’s numbers include listings tagged with phrases like “correct AI,” “AI hallucination,” and “AI error.” The most common category was graphic design, with video editing, proofreading, and content writing following. Each platform measures something different. Freelancer.com counts listings, Upwork tracks gigs, and Fiverr looks at keyword searches. Because of these differences, the figures can’t be directly compared.

Three Different Signals Of AI Cleanup Demand

These figures aren’t directly comparable. Each platform measured a different signal over a different period.

Platform What It Measured Reported Change Period Freelancer.com What It Measured Cleanup job listings Reported Change Up 87%, reaching 10,760 Period August 2025–June 2026 Upwork What It Measured AI remediation gigs Reported Change Up 70% Period Year over year Fiverr What It Measured Searches for “AI cleanup” services Reported Change More than 20x Period 2023–2026 Source: The Guardian , citing data shared by Freelancer.com, Upwork, and Fiverr. A study published in Management Science found demand for some freelance writing and coding work fell after ChatGPT launched. Job posts for the writing and coding jobs most exposed to automation fell 21%, compared with jobs less exposed to it, within eight months of the launch. Posts for image creation fell 17% after image generators arrived. Freelancer.com’s 2025 annual report put average bids per project at 54, up 8% on the prior year.

Cleanup Can Take As Long As Original Work

Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, told the newspaper the work often comes from small companies and entrepreneurs who use AI for a first pass and then hit problems they can’t solve themselves. The time and money saved on the draft, he said, can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use.

Todd Van Linda, a full-time illustrator in Florida, told the outlet one client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book and expected each to take about 15 minutes. He turned it down. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there,” he said.

Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on the side, said he spent two to three hours in Photoshop on each card in a roughly 100-image AI-generated tarot deck with extra fingers and two left feet. Some jobs he turns away. “I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.”

A cheap AI first draft might still require freelancer hours before it’s ready to use, and the freelancers in the Guardian’s report say those hours can equal what original work takes. Last week, another concern arose when reports suggested Google’s August spam update may have targeted mass-produced SEO content generated by AI. Google hasn’t named that as the update’s focus as of publication.

Back in March, I discussed YouTube’s challenge with AI-generated content , focusing on how platforms might spot and demote low-quality videos. On the flip side, the Guardian’s platform stats reveal a different part of the same industry, where companies hire folks to refine AI results before they go out.

The freelancers in the report have different views about how long the work will last. Kym Dunbar, an Australian writer and editor, expects much of the humanizing work to dry up within five to 10 years as models get better. Nathan McConnell, the multimedia editor, shares that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes that might slip past an untrained eye. Lisa, a graphic designer from Spain who asked the outlet not to publish her full name, predicts AI will match her in logo and packaging design within “another year or two.”

Van Linda stopped taking cleanup gigs late last year and said clients unhappy with AI results have since come to him for hand-drawn work instead.

Key Takeaways

  • Meta descriptions aren’t a direct ranking factor, but they influence click-through rate (CTR), which can affect your SEO success. 
  • Google rewrites roughly 70 percent of meta descriptions, but the 30 percent it keeps are your best shot at controlling your search snippet. 
  • Google measures snippet length in pixels, not characters. Aim for 150 to 155 characters and front-load the most important information in the first 110. 
  • Study top-performing paid ads for your target keyword. Repeated phrases can reveal the benefits and language advertisers believe will attract clicks.

You spent time crafting what you thought was a great meta description for your page. You agonized over word choice and character count for what felt like hours, only to have Google ignore it and choose a random sentence from your content to display as the search snippet. 

Why?

The short answer is that Google rewrites roughly 70 percent of meta descriptions. A stat like that may have you wondering if it’s even worth writing them on your own.

It is. The 30 percent of descriptions that Google doesn’t rewrite are your best shot at controlling your first impression in search. My team and I have also discovered that the surviving descriptions share a few common traits.

This guide covers those traits, or meta description best practices. I’ll show you what can earn you clicks in 2026, backed by real examples from brands doing it well. By the end, you’ll have a framework you can take to your business immediately.

What Is a Meta Description?

A meta description is a short HTML tag that summarizes the page’s content.

Readers can’t see meta descriptions or title tags for SEO without inspecting the code.

This meta tag’s importance shows up in the snippet on the search engine results page, below the page URL and title.  

Its job: to show readers what the page offers and persuade them to click. That’s why people often call it a page’s elevator pitch.

Are Meta Descriptions a Ranking Factor?

The short answer is no. Meta descriptions aren’t a direct ranking factor, and Google has confirmed this explicitly through its search advocate, John Mueller, as well as its own search documentation.

However, many SEOs believe that following meta description best practices can indirectly improve rankings. This is based on the assumptions that:

  • Compelling meta descriptions improve click-through rates (CTRs).
  • CTRs are a user signal that Google considers when ranking pages. More people clicking on your page signals to Google that it satisfies their search intent.
  • Well-written meta descriptions improve the user experience. They show readers what they can find on the page and help them decide if they want to visit it. If they do, they’re less likely to bounce, and bounce rates are a quality signal for Google.

That all sounds logical, but no recent large-scale studies confirm the positive impact of meta descriptions on CTR or traffic. Experiments conducted by SEOTesting indicated that optimizing meta descriptions had little effect on traffic, and a case study by SearchPilot showed that removing them improved CTRs.

So why write them at all? 

When Google does use your description, a well-written one that follows meta description best practices for SEO gives you real control over your snippet. Google will use your description when it “describes your page better than other parts of the content.”

A strong meta description can also influence how your page appears on social media. Platforms like Facebook and LinkedIn use a protocol called Open Graph (OG) tags to pull in a page’s title, description, and preview image when someone shares a link.

Key takeaways

  1. Social media goals should tie directly to business objectives like revenue, brand awareness, or customer retention.

What are social media goals?

Social media goals are the desired outcomes you want your social media efforts to achieve. They give your strategy direction and help you measure whether your work is paying off.

It helps to understand how goals, objectives, and tactics relate to each other.

  • Goals are the broad outcomes you’re working toward (like “increase brand awareness”)
  • Social media objectives are the specific, measurable targets within those goals (like “grow Instagram followers by 25% in Q2”)
  • Tactics are the actions you take to get there (like running a branded hashtag campaign)

When all three are aligned, your team knows exactly what success looks like and how to get there.

Bonus: Get a free social media analytics report template  that shows you the most important metrics to track for each network.

Why do social media goals matter?

Social media goals matter because they give your strategy focus and make it possible to measure results. Without them, it’s hard to know whether your efforts are contributing to the business or just generating activity.

For enterprise teams especially, clearly defined goals are the foundation of a scalable social strategy, making it easier to secure budget, align cross-functional stakeholders, and report performance to the C-suite. Shared social media strategy goals also give marketing, communications, and customer care teams a single definition of success to work from. They also help you:

  • Manage your budget,
  • Structure and streamline your workflow,
  • Prove your marketing’s return on investment,
  • Align your social media activity with your organization’s broader business objectives.

Goals can have added benefits like growing your social following, but that shouldn’t be your main motivator.

How do you set social media goals in 5 steps?

Setting effective social media goals doesn’t have to be a mystery. And social media goal setting is a skill you’ll use in many other facets of your career, like when you create a social media proposal.

Here are the five steps at a glance:

  1. Align goals with your business objectives
  2. Use the SMART framework
  3. Identify your key metrics and KPIs
  4. Plan your tactics
  5. Execute, measure, and optimize

Step 1: Align goals with your business objectives

Before you start throwing ideas out there, ask yourself: What problems does our business need to solve? Or, what would most benefit the business in the next year?

Maybe the answer is, “Our business isn’t as recognizable as we would like.” Or “Our business could really use some more web conversions.” If your organization is expanding into a new region, your social goals might focus on building brand awareness in that market.

Your social media goals should be aligned with your business objectives. So, if your business is often confused with your competitors, you can use your social media pages to show people how you’re different and build up your brand’s reputation.

Let your business objectives inform your social media goals.

Step 2: Use the SMART framework

Once you’ve finished step one, make sure the goals you’ve set are attainable. You can do so using the SMART framework.

The SMART framework is a great litmus test for whether or not your goals can be reasonably achieved.

Make sure all of your social media goals are:

  • Specific: Clearly define what you want to accomplish.
  • Measurable: Ensure you can track progress with metrics.
  • Achievable: Set realistic goals that can be attained with your resources.
  • Relevant: Goals should contribute to your business’s broader objectives (see Step 1).
  • Time-bound: Work towards deadlines to keep efforts focused.

articles.title: Social media image sizes for all networks [September 2026]
articles.fullContent:
Social media image sizes seem to change… a lot. And using the wrong dimensions can hurt reach, engagement, and brand consistency. 

This guide covers the current image size requirements for every major social platform in 2026.

Key takeaways

  1. Most social platforms still work best with images that are 1080 pixels wide, especially for feed and full-screen formats.
  2. Vertical, mobile-first aspect ratios like 4:5 and 9:16 now outperform square images on most networks.
  3. Tools like Perch by Hootsuite support network-specific resizing, making it easier for teams to stay consistent as specs change.

Quick social media image sizes

We go into more detail for every single network below, but this image includes the social media image sizes you probably look up most often.

Basic Instagram image sizes

  • Profile photo: 320 x 320 px
  • Landscape: 1080 x 566 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1350 px
  • Square: 1080 x 1080
  • Stories and Reels: 1080 x 1920

Basic Facebook image sizes

  • Profile photo: 196 x 196 px
  • Landscape: 1080 x 566 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1359 px
  • Square: 1080 x 1080 px
  • Stories and Reels: 1080 x 1920 px
  • Cover photo: 851 x 315 px

Basic X (formerly Twitter) image sizes

  • Profile photo: 400 x 400 px
  • Landscape: 1280 x 720 px
  • Vertical: 720 x 1280 px
  • Square: 720 x 720 px
  • Cover photo: 1500 x 500 px

Basic LinkedIn image sizes

  • Profile photo: 400 x 400 px
  • Landscape: 1200 x 627 px
  • Vertical: 720 x 900 px
  • Square: 1200 x 1200 px
  • Cover photo size: 1128 x 191 px

Basic TikTok image sizes

  • Profile photo: 20 x 20 px
  • Landscape (ad): 1920 x 1080 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1920 px
  • Square (ad): 640 x 640 px
  • Stories: 1080 x 1920 px

Instagram image sizes

Instagram supports horizontally and vertically oriented images well as square images. Well, sort of. You can still use all of these photo orientations in your posts, and that’s how they’ll appear in the Instagram feed. But they will all be displayed with a vertical crop on your Instagram grid.

This makes image dimensions a little tricky to get right, especially if you want to control the look of your grid as a cohesive whole. Follow these guidelines to make sure your images end up looking their best.

Instagram profile picture size: 320 x 320 pixels

Instagram profile photos are displayed at 110 x 100 pixels, but the image files are stored at 320 x 320 pixels, so make sure to upload an image that’s at least that big.

Even though the dimensions are in a square format, Instagram profile photos are displayed as a circle. Make sure any elements you want to focus on in the photo are centered so they don’t get cropped out.

Instagram post sizes:

  • Landscape image: 1080 x 566 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Vertical image: 1080 x 1350 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Square image: 1080 x 1080 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Carousel images: 1080 x 1350 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Supported aspect ratios: Anywhere between 1.91:1 and 4:5 (feed) / 3:4 (grid)
  • Recommended image size: Width of 1080 pixels, height between 566 and 1350 pixels

Tips:

  • If you want your images to look their best on Instagram, aim to upload an image that is 1080 pixels wide.
  • When you share an Instagram image that’s sized over 1080 pixels, Instagram will size it down to 1080 pixels.
  • If you share a photo that has a resolution lower than 320 pixels, Instagram will size it up to 320 pixels.
  • If your image is between 320 and 1080 pixels wide, Instagram will keep that photo at its original resolution, “as long as the photo’s aspect ratio is between 1.91:1 and 4:5 (a height between 566 and 1350 pixels with a width of 1080 pixels).”
  • If you upload an image using a different ratio, the platform will automatically crop your photo to fit a supported ratio.
  • Remember that all photos appear in vertical format on your grid.

articles.title: Social media marketing for CPG brands: A 2026 playbook
articles.fullContent:
Got a product on the shelves? That’s a huge win, but it’s far from over. Now you need to move it off the shelves, and do it consistently.

Social media marketing for CPG is how you make that happen. Here’s everything you need to know.

Key takeaways

  1. Social turns everyday products into memorable brands. It helps CPG brands build a personality, stay top-of-mind, and create social proof
  2. Different platforms do different jobs. TikTok is built for discovery, Instagram for visual storytelling, YouTube for education, and Facebook for reach.
  3. Hootsuite helps CPG teams stay organized. Perch centralizes planning and scheduling across brands, while Lumen helps teams track sentiment, reviews, and category trends.

Why does social media marketing matter for CPG brands?

For CPG brands, social media turns everyday products into brands people actually remember and reach for.

Here are a few reasons why social matters:

  • It gives your brand a personality. Two cans of sparkling water may not be that different from one another. Social is where you can make yours feel different with a clear personality and point of view.
  • It keeps you top-of-mind. If people keep seeing your product or messaging in their feeds, you have a better shot at being the one they remember in the aisle.
  • It provides social proof. Seeing real people recommend a product makes it feel less risky to try, and lends it more credibility.
  • It works across the funnel. The same platform can help people discover your product, give them reasons to consider it, and even close the sale.
  • It doubles as free research. Every comment, share, or search is a glimpse into how people actually talk about your category (and what they care about). 

Which brings us to the simplest reason of all: your consumers are already on social, so you should be there too.

“Social’s not just an important channel these days, it’s table stakes,” says Alli Meyer, Fractional Brand, Trade, and Consumer Insights Director at AM Marketing Strategy. 

“If you don’t have a presence on social media, or much of one, you don’t exist for most of your consumers,” she adds. “And this cuts across generations, not just digital natives, because all consumers use social media.”

Do it better with Hootsuite, the all-in-one social media tool. Stay on top of things, grow, and beat the competition.

What platforms should CPG brands prioritize?

CPG brands should prioritize the platforms where their customers already spend time. From there, it helps to know what each one does well.

Here’s a quick rundown:

TikTok: Best for discovery and creator partnerships

83% of shoppers say they’ve discovered a new product on TikTok, and 70% have discovered a new brand. 

Creators are a big reason for that. User-generated content (like tutorials and unboxings) is everywhere on the app, drumming up tons of organic exposure. 

Brands can add fuel to the fire with paid partnerships. Beauty brand Sacheu Beauty, for example, works with thousands of creators on TikTok, and they drive 90% of its sales.

Source: @gingerpixie03

Instagram: Best for visual storytelling

CPG marketing is inherently visual. From packaging to product photos, half the pitch is just letting people see the thing. 

That makes Instagram, the OG image-first platform, an easy pick.

articles.fullContent:
As social media users spread their attention across multiple platforms, more brands are expanding their presence to meet them there. According to our 2026 Social Media Content Strategy report, 87% of marketers plan to show up on more networks this year.

Cross-posting on social media is an excellent strategy for reaching new audiences, but it can also multiply your team’s workload, especially if you’re tailoring content to each platform.

This guide explains what cross-posting is, when it works (or backfires) and what each platform’s native rules allow. You’ll also learn how to cross-post easily with the Sprout Social Essentials plan.

What is cross-posting on social media?

Cross-posting means publishing the same content to two or more social media networks, either simultaneously or on a network-specific schedule.

But your posts shouldn’t be identical across platforms. A good cross-posting strategy preserves the core message or creative concept while optimizing the size, caption, format, tags, media and timing for each channel.

When you cross-post on social media effectively, you get content on your brand accounts quickly, freeing up your team for more strategic tasks like planning and engaging.

The right tools simplify the process. Sprout Social Essentials lets you cross-post to up to five social profiles at once. Use the unified Compose window to customize your post’s text, media and timing for each platform—no switching tabs.

Cross-posting vs. reposting vs. repurposing vs. sharing

Cross-posting, reposting, repurposing and sharing all extend the reach of your social content, but they describe different actions.

  • Cross-posting is when you publish your own content to several networks you control, with or without channel-specific editing.
  • Reposting is when you republish an existing post, yours or someone else’s, in its original form and usually within the same network.
  • Repurposing is when you rebuild an asset into one or several new formats to extend its life, increase reach and maximize ROI.
  • Sharing is when you distribute someone else’s post, either on your feed or to someone’s private inbox, through a native sharing button.

Here’s a quick table with examples of each term:

Term What it means Example Cross-posting Publishing one core post across multiple networks at the same time (or on an automated schedule) Publishing a ‘New Arrivals’ post on Instagram, LinkedIn and Facebook Reposting Resurfacing an existing post, yours or someone else’s, usually within the same network Reposting a customer’s Instagram post on your brand profile Repurposing Turning one asset into several different formats or deliverables Converting a webinar into three Reels and a LinkedIn carousel Sharing Distributing someone else’s post through a native sharing button Sharing a partner’s post to your feed or sending it through a direct message

Should you post the same content on every network?

Only cross-post content to networks where the topic is relevant and the format makes sense. Even then, “same content” should mean the same idea, not an untouched copy of the same post.

Exact duplication works for simple, time-sensitive updates. But for most campaigns, small changes to the hook, caption, tags, call-to-action, media and publish time give the post a better chance of meeting each audience’s expectations.

When cross-posting works well

Cross-posting works well when speed and consistency matter, or when audiences have similar needs across channels. Examples of content to cross-post include:

  • Company and product announcements: Launch dates, new locations, event registrations and important service updates benefit from a consistent message.
  • Evergreen education: Tips, how-to content, FAQs and research findings are useful across several networks, especially with minor tweaks.
  • Short-form video: A clean, watermark-free vertical video works across Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts.
  • Little to no audience overlap: If research shows your audience varies across platforms, cross-posting helps you reach more people without looking repetitive.

As for cadence, cross-post as often as the content fits each network, but balance it with platform-specific posts so every feed still feels original and worth following.

When to tailor or skip cross-posting

Create a separate post or stick to one network only when the content relies heavily on platform-specific behavior. Skip cross-posting in the following situations:

  • Format mismatch: A text-only update has no direct equivalent on TikTok, while a 10-minute landscape video won’t work on Instagram.
  • Overlapping audiences: Followers who see identical posts on several networks in quick succession will tune them out. Change the hook or stagger the timing.
  • Unique native features: Not every network supports features like polls, in-app sounds, stickers, live video, collaboration tools and document posts.
  • Varying audience expectations: Avoid cross-posting when content is built around platform-specific trends or needs a different angle, such as the business impact of an announcement on LinkedIn versus its human side on Instagram.

In these scenarios, the cons of cross-posting outweigh the pros. But that doesn’t mean cross-posting is bad for performance. Just avoid sharing identical or poorly adapted posts all the time as it makes your brand look repetitive and boring.

Benefits of cross-posting to multiple social channels

Cross-posting makes executing and scaling a multi-channel marketing strategy effortless. These five benefits show where cross-posting has the greatest impact.

Market to different target demographics

Cross-posting helps your brand reach different customer groups without recreating content from scratch every single time.

Every network has its own mix of age groups, interests, professions and behaviors. For example, the latest social media demographics show that Facebook reaches 88% of Baby Boomers, compared with 39% for Instagram and 20% for TikTok.

If you’re a sports brand targeting both older and younger customers, you can cross-post a vertical video to all three platforms, tweaking the caption to resonate more with each audience.

What is user-generated content (UGC)?

User-generated content (UGC) is original, brand-specific content created by real customers and fans rather than by the brand itself. It can come in many forms, including videos, images, product reviews, testimonials, and even podcasts.

UGC can live everywhere: your own social channels, third-party review sites (e.g., Google and G2), community forums, blogs, or on your customers’ own social profiles.

When a happy customer posts about your product and you reshare it — like in the example below from drink brand Wildwonder — that’s UGC in action.

What are the different types of user-generated content?

UGC comes in two main flavors: organic and paid. Both can show up as customer reviews, photos, videos, social media posts, or blog posts — the difference is whether money changed hands.

What is organic UGC?

Organic UGC is content your real customers share freely, without being paid or asked. It’s the most authentic type of UGC, and the kind every brand hopes to see more of.

Here are a few examples of organic UGC:

Reviews and testimonials

Online reviews are a classic form of UGC, and they work hard as social proof across your website and social channels.

Some brands even turn glowing testimonials into branded graphics to share on social. It’s an easy way to squeeze more value out of a single review.

Photos

Photos are one of the most common types of UGC. Think: A customer showing off your product in the wild, or sharing their results after using it.

Use a niche or branded hashtag to make these posts easier to find (and reshare) later.

For example, footwear brand Asics uses the hashtag #soundmindsoundbody to collect photos from fans around the world. One quick search pulls up thousands of posts they can tap into for both content and community-building.

Videos

Social videos and YouTube content are UGC gold. YouTubers regularly post “product hauls” or unboxing videos featuring multiple brands in one video. If yours gets a mention, grab that clip (with permission) and feature it on your own channels.

Social media posts

Even a quick, positive mention of your brand is worth resharing. Repost it directly on X or TikTok, or take a screenshot and turn it into a graphic for Instagram and LinkedIn. Hootsuite’s engagement tools make it easy to spot these moments as they happen.

Blog posts

Bloggers may also shout your brand out, whether it’s a full review or a passing mention in a bigger roundup. Pull a quote and share it on social or your website to extend its reach.

For example, travel blogger Nikki on Her Way casually recommends Tevas as the best brand for water shoes in her long-term packing guide. It’s a quick, unprompted endorsement that Teva could easily pull into their own content marketing.

Paid UGC is content made by creators you hire to talk about your product. It’s a popular option for newer brands that don’t have a big customer base sharing content organically (yet).

According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, 39% of Australian social users turn to TikTok to keep up with trends in many areas, from finance to fashion, technology to travel. For businesses, this level of engagement represents a major marketing opportunity—but only if they know exactly how and why Australians are using the app.

What started as an entertainment feed now shapes how Australians discover products, research big decisions and connect with the brands they love. Marketers who understand that shift meet their audience where attention already lives and turn casual scrolling into real business results.

In this guide, we cover the most important TikTok statistics in Australia to help you build a smarter, data-led strategy. With these insights, you can guide your social strategy, spark TikTok campaign ideas and create content that truly resonates with Australian audiences.

Key TikTok statistics in Australia

TikTok is a major player in Australia’s social media landscape. As of late 2025, 10.9 million Australians aged 18 and over use the app, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report. These statistics show how deeply the network has embedded itself into everyday life:

  • More than 350,000 Australian businesses use TikTok, restated by the company in 2026.

  • Australian users spend an average of 1 hour 14 minutes a day in the app (August 2025), the highest daily figure of any social app in Australia, per DataReportal and We Are Social.

  • According to Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report, short-form videos (<60 seconds long) perform best on TikTok. Users are most interested in entertaining content, product discovery and influencer partnerships

  • TikTok ads reached 51.2% of Australian adults aged 18 and over at the end of 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Australia counted 21.0 million social media user identities in October 2025, equal to 77.7% of the population, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to a 2024 report from Oxford Economics, 19% of Australian users have donated to a charity or cause they saw on TikTok, and 18% have committed their time to volunteer.

articles.title: Social media optimization: 15 proven tactics for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media optimization improves reach, engagement, and conversions. It works by refining your profiles, content, and posting strategy based on data, not guesswork.
  2. Discoverability is now driven by social search. Keywords, hashtags, and profile optimization matter more than ever as people search directly inside social apps.
  3. A structured approach covers five areas. Optimize for engagement, growth, conversions, accessibility, and overall performance rather than chasing one metric.
  4. Scaling optimization requires centralized tools. Managing posting times, hashtags, analytics, and content across networks from one platform saves time and improves consistency.

What is social media optimization?

Social media optimization is the process of improving your social media content, profiles, and strategies to achieve better results: faster follower growth, higher levels of engagement, more clicks or conversions, and so on.

SMO covers both the small, tactical improvements you make to individual posts and the bigger strategic decisions behind your presence, like which platforms you invest in and what your content mix looks like.

Common tactics of social media optimization include:

  • Basic improvements to individual posts, such as adding a call-to-action in a caption or picking a scroll-stopping visual
  • Larger strategic improvements, like redefining your brand’s tone of voice on social media
  • Optimizing posting times and frequency based on audience behavior
  • Improving discoverability, such as adding keywords to bios and captions so your content surfaces in social search

That last point matters more each year. Social platforms increasingly function as discovery and search engines, so optimization is no longer just about pleasing a feed algorithm. It’s about being findable.

In any case, social media optimization should be based on performance analysis, audience research, and insights gathered through social listening.

Bonus !!!

Bonus: Get a free social media strategy template to quickly and easily plan your strategy, track results, and share with your boss, teammates, and clients.

How does social media optimization relate to SEO?

Social media optimization and SEO share the same goal: making your brand easier to find. The difference is where that discovery happens. SEO improves your visibility in search engines like Google, while SMO improves your visibility inside social platforms, in feeds, recommendations, and in-app search.

The two also support each other. Social content can drive branded searches, earn links when other sites pick up your posts, and extend the life of blog content you’ve already optimized. And because platforms like TikTok and Instagram now behave like search engines themselves, many of the same habits apply: research what people are looking for, use their language, and structure content so it’s easy to categorize.

Social media automation is the process of letting tools handle routine and repetitive tasks like scheduling posts or tracking brand mentions.   • As of 2026, 59.8% of users identified as male and 39.7% as female.

  • International daily users (77.1 million) now outpace US daily users (53.2 million) and are growing around 28% a year.

articles.title: How to conduct a customer experience audit rooted in social intelligence
articles.fullContent:
Your customers are already telling you where their experience is falling short. The problem is, they don’t always tell you directly.

They post about it on social media, ask questions in comments, leave Google and Yelp reviews and talk about your brand in places your customer experience team may never see. Those conversations can expose frustrations, unmet needs and changing expectations that traditional feedback channels miss.

A customer experience audit gives you a structured way to evaluate those interactions across the customer journey. Building social intelligence into the process keeps the audit grounded in what customers are saying now and helps you decide what needs attention first.

In this article, we’ll break down what a customer experience audit involves, where social intelligence fits in and how to use the findings to improve the customer journey.

What is a customer experience audit?

A customer experience audit is a structured review of how people interact with your brand across the customer journey. It examines the touchpoints and feedback that shape the experience, from initial discovery through purchase and support.

Think of it like a health check for your customer experience. You’re looking at how different parts of the journey work together and where friction shows up between channels or departments.

A strong CX audit also looks beyond the channels your business owns. Social conversations and customer care interactions add context that surveys or CRM data alone may not capture, giving you a stronger foundation for what to improve.

5 steps for a modern customer experience audit that drives action

A customer experience audit works best when you approach it systematically. Here’s how to move from deciding what you want to learn to tracking whether your changes are working.

1. Set expectations for your CX audit

Before you pull data or review touchpoints, set the audit parameters. The steps below will help you establish what you’re trying to accomplish and what it will take to get there.

Involve the right stakeholders

Customer experience rarely sits with one department. Bring in people who own different parts of the journey, such as customer care, CX, social, marketing, PR and data analysts. Each group may catch gaps others miss.

Clarify everyone’s role upfront, too. Decide who will lead the audit, who will provide data or context and who needs to act on the findings.

Determine objectives and goals

Next, decide what you want to learn or improve. You might be trying to understand why customers abandon checkout after clicking through from social, improve response times on social or figure out where the brand experience feels inconsistent across channels.

Tie those objectives to specific parts of the customer journey and the outcomes that matter most. This will guide which touchpoints and metrics you review later.

Define scope

A CX audit can expand quickly across channels, customer groups and stages of the journey, so set boundaries before you begin.

Based on your objectives, decide what needs attention now based on your specific business priorities. That might mean auditing one priority audience across the full lifecycle or zeroing in on a stage where you already know there’s friction. Future audits can broaden the scope as new questions arise.

2. Map the customer journey across touch points

Customer journeys rarely follow a neat, predictable path. People move between channels and platforms as they discover brands, weigh their options and get support, making it harder to see the full experience in one place.

Mapping those touchpoints reveals how the pieces connect and where social media plays a role.

Capture the full customer lifecycle from discovery through care

Social influences customers at several key points in their relationship with your brand:

  • Product discovery: According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, around a third of consumers prefer social search for product reviews.
  • Purchase: Sprout’s State of Influencer Marketing Report found that 86% of consumers make an influencer-inspired purchase at least once a year.
  • Customer care: The Sprout Social Index™ found that 73% of social media users expect brands to respond on social within 24 hours.

Mapping your social media marketing funnel alongside the broader customer journey helps account for those interactions from discovery through ongoing social customer care.

Look beyond owned channels

Build your audit from the places customers interact with or talk about your brand. Alongside your own social posts and ads, include replies, DMs, chatbot interactions, reviews, customer posts, social shopping activity and traffic from social to your website. Widen the lens to review sites, discussion forums, influencer communities, media coverage and mentions that may never reach your profiles.

Sprout helps bring more of those touchpoints into one workflow. The Smart Inbox centralizes incoming social messages, while Reviews pulls customer feedback from sources including Google Business Profile, Yelp, Trustpilot and TripAdvisor. Sprout Social Listening bridges direct and indirect interactions, surfacing conversations about your brand and market that may not tag or mention you directly. Together, these tools give you a broader pool of customer conversations to draw from during the audit.

Connect social with the systems other teams use, too. The Sprout Social Salesforce integration enriches CRM profiles with social data, while Sprout’s Tableau BI Connector combines social with other business data for a fuller view of the journey.

3. Use social intelligence to identify pain points and gaps in customer experience

With the customer journey mapped, it’s time to diagnose what’s happening within it. Where is frustration building? What questions keep coming up? Are expectations changing faster than your experience can keep pace with?

Social intelligence helps answer those questions by illustrating how customer sentiment and conversation patterns are changing across the market.

Analyze audience sentiment

Look at how customers feel at key points in the journey. A drop in sentiment around a product launch or an increase in negative customer care messages can point to experiences worth investigating.

Social listening helps track sentiment across broader conversations, while Sprout’s Sentiment for Messages classifies incoming messages and reviews, enabling teams to identify interactions that need attention. NewsWhip by Sprout Social further adds predictive media intelligence to indicate when stories or issues are gaining traction.

Facebook ad targeting is the system within Meta Ads Manager that lets advertisers define exactly who sees your ads. Meta decides the winner using a total value score built from several inputs:

  • Audience settings: Who you’ve made your ad eligible to reach, whether that’s a Core audience, a Custom Audience, or a broad Advantage+ pool.

  • Ad quality and relevance: Signals from your creative, engagement history, and feedback from people who have seen similar ads.

AI is starting to change the equation. Social media tasks that once ate up entire afternoons can increasingly be delegated to AI agents and automated workflows. The question isn’t simply what social teams can automate, but what must be automated to keep up.

This article breaks down which tasks are best handed off to AI, where human judgment still matters and how automation can give social teams more room to focus on higher-value work.

Social media manager tasks: A daily overview

A social media manager’s day covers a lot more than planning content and hitting publish. Here are some social media tasks that fall under most social media job titles:

  • Respond to comments and messages across platforms

  • Curate and create engaging content
  • Schedule posts for the next day, week or month
  • Analyze metrics to gauge performance
  • Brainstorm content ideas
  • Research trending topics and conversations
  • Manage paid social media campaigns
  • Vet and coordinate with creators and influencers
  • Handle crisis communication, as needed

Which of these are you still doing manually? Look at each task and ask: Could AI handle it? Or does it still need a person’s judgment?

Automated tasks in social media marketing: What AI can do now

A few years ago, most social media tasks required a person at every step. Now, AI handles a growing share of the daily workload, from scheduling to reporting to the first pass on customer replies.

Publishing & scheduling

Getting a post approved and published can often involve a few rounds of email or Slack follow-ups with your manager or other stakeholders. Automated approval workflows remove that back-and-forth by sending content directly to the right person at the right stage.

Choosing when to post has also become more precise. Instead of relying on generic best-practice windows, AI can analyze when your specific audience is most likely to engage. Sprout’s Optimal Send Times with ViralPost uses your audience’s behavior to recommend the best publishing times.

Alt text is another task that can slip when deadlines get tight. AI can help by generating descriptive alt text within the publishing workflow, making accessibility easier to build into the process. Sprout’s Generate ALT Text capability does this directly in the platform.

Reporting & insights

AI can cut down that work by letting teams query social data in plain language instead of rebuilding the analysis from scratch each time. With Sprout’s Trellis, social teams, leaders and cross-functional partners can ask questions about social performance and get answers without waiting for someone to pull a report.

Social listening & media intelligence

Within Sprout Listening, Trellis takes that a step further by letting teams ask questions about sentiment, share of voice or emerging themes in plain language and get answers based on their listening data.

AI can also help teams spot reputation risks earlier. NewsWhip by Sprout Social analyzes real-time signals across social and the web to predict which stories are likely to gain traction. Teams get an earlier read on what’s picking up steam and more time to decide how to respond.

Finding the right creators can take hours of scrolling profiles and comparing audiences to see if someone is a good fit for the brand. AI speeds up that research by narrowing a large pool of creators to a smaller set based on specific criteria.

Creator managers can spend less time on manual research and more time reviewing the strongest options, reaching out and building relationships.

Customer messages don’t stop at the end of the day, and some need attention faster than others. AI can help care teams triage incoming comments and DMs by analyzing sentiment and identifying messages that may need a quicker response.

It can also draft responses for customer care agents to review and personalize, accelerating personalization while cutting down the time spent writing routine replies from scratch.

AI can pull data, spot patterns and draft a response. But it can’t navigate internal politics, interpret culture, earn trust or persuade a leader to invest more in social.

Automating routine work gives social teams more time for the parts of the job that depend on judgment, context and relationships.

Getting another team to act on social insights takes more than sending them a report. Social leaders need to understand what product, customer care or sales is trying to solve, then connect social data to the decisions already on their plate.

articles.title: The Practical Guide to Google Analytics 4
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Google renamed “Conversions” to “Key Events” in 2024. The terms mean different things in GA4 and Google Ads, so getting the terminology right matters when comparing numbers across platforms. 
  • Every interaction in GA4 is event-based, with parameters providing the context behind what happened.
  • Data-driven attribution is GA4’s default model, using machine learning to spread credit across all the touchpoints that led to a conversion. 
  • BigQuery export is free for standard properties and unlocks analysis that the standard reports can’t handle. 
  • DebugView is the fastest way to catch broken tracking before it becomes weeks of unusable data.

Are you getting the most out of Google Analytics 4 (GA4)?

GA4 has been Google’s standard analytics platform for a few years now. The move from Universal Analytics (UA) was a major shift, but Google has continued updating GA4 itself along the way. One of the biggest changes came in 2024, when Google replaced “Conversions” with “Key Events” in 2024. 

While some marketers might miss UA, there’s no going back.

This GA4 guide skips the history lesson and focuses on what you need to do in GA4 day to day, from proper setup to tracking key events (not conversions) and other impactful metrics.

What Is Google Analytics 4?

Google Analytics 4 is the current version of Google Analytics, and it provides web analytics on a level that allows marketers to effectively analyze important customer usage metrics, not just track traffic.

Before we get into the details, here’s a quick Google Analytics 4 overview. 

Google Analytics 4 tracks the entire customer path across multiple platforms and leverages AI and machine learning to provide more detailed insights into how users interact with your website and app.

GA4 combines cross-channel measurement and AI-driven predictive analytics. It also operates under a privacy-first tracking framework designed for today’s privacy laws, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). 

These features combine to give marketers a more complete view of how users interact with their digital properties than what UA offered.

How to Set Up Google Analytics 4

Many marketers ask me how to use GA4. Your setup process will depend on whether you’re tracking a website or an app (or both). I’ve broken down each option below.

Google Analytics for Firebase

Firebase is Google’s app development platform that helps you build and deploy apps and games. If you enable Google Analytics when creating a Firebase project, Firebase automatically links your app to a GA4 property.  

If you’re working with an older Firebase project, you may need to link it to a GA4 property or complete Google’s upgrade process.

To upgrade your Firebase account to Google Analytics 4, follow these steps:

  1. Log in to the Firebase console.
  2. Go to Analytics > Dashboard on the left panel.
  3. Follow any prompts to enable or upgrade GA for the project. 

Once linked, you can find app analytics in both the Firebase console and Google Analytics.

Setting up Google Analytics 4 from Scratch

If you’ve never used Google Analytics before or you want to set up a brand-new website, you’ll need to start from scratch:

  • Create an Analytics account if you haven’t already by visiting https://analytics.google.com and opening Admin. Then click Create, and then Account (skip if you already have an account).
  • In the Property column, click Create > Property.
  • Enter a name for your new property, and select a time zone and currency. 
  • Select your industry category and business size.
  • Select your business objectives (e.g., “Get baseline reports,” “Generate leads”).
  • Click Create and accept the Terms of Service.
  • Add a data stream (Web, iOS, or Android) to start collecting data.

Source: https://www.eridesignstudio.com/insights/set-up-a-google-analytics-4-property/

A data stream is a source of information that feeds your GA4 analytics property. It could be your website or your app. Google will guide you through adding each data stream.

Install With Google Tag Manager

For most marketers, Google Tag Manager (GTM) is the recommended installation method. GTM lets you deploy and update the GA4 tag (along with other marketing tags) without touching the site code whenever something changes.

To set up, create a free GTM account and add a container for your site. Google will give you two snippets of code to paste on every page (one in the <head>, one right after the opening <body> tag). 

Once the container is live, create a Google tag inside GTM using your GA4 Measurement ID and set it to fire on all pages. Publish the container to push your changes live.

Verify With DebugView

After setup, use DebugView (found under Admin) to confirm your events are firing correctly. It shows real-time event data from a single device with debug mode enabled, which beats waiting for reports to populate. Skipping this step is a common way for broken tracking to go unnoticed for weeks.

articles.title: How to manage social media as a one-person team
articles.fullContent:
As the hub of cultural conversations and online activity, social media provides valuable intelligence to inform business strategies. It’s how you discover everything from what trends are taking over to what products people are buying. In fact, the 2026 Social Intelligence Report found that half of one-person teams consider it mission-critical for future growth.

But between crafting content and staying on top of communications, managing social media is hard enough when you’re the only one on the team. This leaves you with little time to focus on social intelligence, let alone extract insights to fuel business growth.

In this post, we provide a guideline on how to streamline social media management for one-person teams. From strategic automation to structured task management, we show you how you can save time and focus on more high-impact work. Let’s get started.

What it means to run social alone

When you’re running social media on your own, you’re juggling multiple roles. You’re the one coming up with content ideas and bringing those ideas to fruition by writing captions and designing graphics. At the same time, you’re in charge of publishing the content, managing comments, responding to DMs and analyzing your data.

You’re essentially doing everything by yourself all at once.

As it is, social media marketers are already at risk of burning out and running out of content ideas. The 2025 Sprout Social Index TM notes that 33% of marketers fear burnout and creative fatigue.

The risk gets significantly bigger for someone who’s constantly overwhelmed because they’re doing it all alone. Yet this is what social media management looks like for most startups and small business operations.

The biggest challenges for a one-person team

To start with, you need to pinpoint what actually makes it challenging to manage social media on your own. That way, you can focus your efforts on tackling those specific challenges. Let’s dig deeper into the biggest problems in social media management for one-person teams.

Constant context-switching across platforms

One minute you’re checking your Facebook stats, the next you’re trying to catch up on all your Instagram DMs and messages. When you’re a one-person social media team, you’re constantly switching between different tasks across platforms. So you’re distracted and unable to focus on a single task, which will affect productivity.

It’s even worse when you’re doing everything manually. According to The Social Media Productivity Report, 63% of social media marketers report not being able to do high-impact work because of manual tasks.

Creative and content fatigue

Social media teams have to always be on top of trending memes and viral topics to keep producing relevant content. According to the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM , 94% of social media practitioners report having to be chronically online to do their jobs.

Ultimately, the social media burnout catches up, especially when you’re the only one coming up with ideas and producing content. That’s why burnout and creative fatigue rank as the fourth greatest fear among social media marketers.

Proving ROI without a dedicated analyst

When you’re the only one on your team, you’re also in charge of collecting performance data and putting together reports. It’s easy enough to point out which content is performing well or how your page has grown over time. But without a dedicated analyst to interpret your data, you’ll have a hard time aligning your social media investment to actual business outcomes.

Keeping up with response-time expectations

Between the content creation and performance analysis, comments and DMs often go unanswered for hours when you’re a one-person team. This could reflect poorly on the customer experience, especially with consumers expecting swift responses on social media.

As the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM found, almost three-quarters of consumers expect brands to respond within 24 hours. They’ll even buy from a competitor next time if the brand doesn’t respond to their customer service questions on social.

3 tips for prioritizing when everything feels urgent

You’re a few days behind on content and your DMs are flooded with messages that you haven’t been able to check. For one-person social teams, it seems like there’s a never-ending to-do list where every item needs to be done “right now.” Here’s how you can streamline your tasks and figure out what to prioritize:

1. Set 2–3 goals tied to business outcomes, not vanity metrics

Impressions are great, but what do they actually mean for your business? Have a clear idea of what you want to get out of social media. This will serve as the foundation for the rest of your social media marketing strategy, shaping everything from your content to your analytics.

Start with 2-3 goals that are related to actual business outcomes. For instance:

  • Growing brand awareness
  • Building a brand community
  • Improving brand sentiment
  • Generating online sales
  • Driving qualified leads
  • Preventing customer churn
  • Speeding up social customer service

2. Use an impact-vs-effort framework to triage daily tasks

Building a framework for prioritizing tasks will help you organize your schedule more strategically. Weigh the expected value of each task against the effort needed to complete it, so you can sort out the order in which to do them.

For example:

Quick wins (high impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require very little time or money
  • Examples: Repurposing existing content into graphics and bite-sized social posts, sharing user-generated content, customizing social media templates for new ideas, actively replying to recent comments

Big bets (high impact, high effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require heavy planning, time and/or budget
  • Examples: Running an influencer marketing campaign, launching a multi-platform content series

Backups (low impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Minor tasks that don’t add significant value but take very little time to complete
